archimate:Folder.name: 3 Business Services
archimate:Folder.documentation:
Within the Business Architecture of the Statistical Architecture Framework (SAF), Business Services represent the formalized interface through which a statistical organization delivers value to its internal and external users. A business service exposes one or more business processes and functions as a coherent, governed, and user-oriented offering that fulfills a specific business need or supports a defined business outcome.
Where business processes describe the flow of work and business functions capture the underlying capabilities, business services define how these internal capabilities are made accessible to stakeholders — transforming operational capabilities into consumable and reusable services. This service-oriented view introduces a structured and modular way for the statistical organization to interact with its environment, whether those interactions occur between internal departments, across government institutions, or with external partners, researchers, and citizens.
A business service can be defined as a contractual representation of value delivery, combining people, processes, information, and resources to provide a specific business outcome. Each service is supported by a set of business functions and realized through one or more business processes, yet remains stable from a user perspective even if the internal mechanisms evolve. This separation between the service interface and its realization is a key architectural principle within SAF, ensuring that modernization and automation of internal processes do not disrupt the way users consume statistical or data-related services.
Business services in the SAF are designed according to three key architectural principles:
Abstraction and Encapsulation: A business service abstracts the complexity of internal processes, exposing only what is necessary for users to access or consume. It encapsulates underlying business logic, ensuring that users interact with clear, predictable interfaces rather than internal workflows or organizational boundaries.
Reusability and Composability: Business services are reusable components that can be orchestrated or combined to deliver more complex value propositions. For example, a “Data Access Service” may be composed of sub-services such as Authorization Management, Data Delivery, and Usage Reporting, each of which can also be used independently by other business processes.
Consistency and Governance: Each business service is governed by a service contract that defines its purpose, scope, inputs, outputs, and conditions of use. This promotes standardization, transparency, and quality assurance, aligning service delivery with the organization’s legal, ethical, and methodological obligations.
Within the context of a statistical organization, business services can take various forms depending on the stakeholder they serve.
Internal business services enable collaboration and coordination across departments — for example, a Metadata Management Service or Process Quality Monitoring Service.
External business services provide value to data users, researchers, policymakers, and the general public — such as a Statistical Data Access Service, Research Support Service, or Secure Processing Environment Access Service.
By exposing processes and functions through well-defined services, the organization transitions from a functionally siloed operation to a service-oriented enterprise. This supports scalability, interoperability, and flexibility, especially in a landscape where statistical organizations increasingly operate as part of national and European data ecosystems or data spaces.
In ArchiMate terms, a business service is realized by business processes and functions, is used by business roles or actors, and produces or manipulates business artefacts. This modeling relationship creates a transparent chain from service demand to service delivery, illustrating how business value is generated, consumed, and governed. Through these relationships, the SAF enables traceability between user needs, service offerings, and underlying capabilities — a critical enabler for modernization and digital transformation.
From an operational perspective, the introduction of a service orientation allows the statistical organization to:
Standardize and catalog its offerings through a business service catalogue;
Improve agility by decoupling service interfaces from process implementations;
Enhance user experience by providing coherent access points to data, metadata, and analytical tools;
Support interoperability by exposing services through APIs or standard protocols aligned with data governance frameworks such as the European Health Data Space (EHDS) or the Common Statistical Data Architecture (CSDA).
Ultimately, the Business Services component of the SAF provides the essential connective tissue between the organization’s internal operations and the external world. It transforms the organization’s capabilities and processes into value-creating, user-oriented offerings that can be governed, measured, and improved. In doing so, it embodies one of the SAF’s key design principles — to make the business architecture actionable, interoperable, and service-driven.
By defining, structuring, and governing its business services, a statistical organization positions itself not just as a producer of statistics, but as a trusted service provider within the broader data ecosystem — capable of delivering consistent, secure, and high-quality data-driven services that support evidence-based policy, research, and innovation.
